extracted.intended_audience: general readers; humorists; public speakers; authors; students of rhetoric and style
extracted.subtask_description: Collected public addresses and humorous essays by Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens) containing satirical arguments about spelling, practical advice for authors and lecturers, and illustrative anecdotal morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real/supreme function of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language's essential or supreme function is 'merely to convey ideas and emotions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If language can convey ideas and emotions with words of phonetic brevity and compactness, then cumbersome, wasteful forms are unnecessary. This principle underlies arguments in favor of simplified spelling and against preserving antiquated orthography for its associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of simplified orthography (phonetic brevity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthography should reduce 'waste letters' and compress phonetics to the minimum necessary to convey meaning and feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain presents a purportedly genuine letter (with idiosyncratic spelling and no punctuation) as proof that simplified spelling can 'convey any fact you need to convey; and it can pour out emotions.' Example features: eliminate surplus letters, favor phonetic forms, and accept minimal punctuation. The letter is used as a rhetorical example showing clarity and emotional force despite nonstandard spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of orthographic reform for immigrants/citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: Spelling should be simplified to aid the large population who must learn English and to avoid delaying immigrants' integration and citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain argues the present orthography is kept to satisfy a small minority (e.g., 'one million people') at the expense of the many (e.g., 'eighty-two millions'), and that modern convenience should outweigh sentimental preservation. This is an explicit utilitarian criterion for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of sentimental argument for preserving archaic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that archaic spelling must be kept because it is 'the spelling of Chaucer and Spencer and Shakespeare' is dismissed as sentimental and not a sound reason for preserving harmful forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain uses analogies (preserving flies/cockroaches in hospitals; preserving a family cancer) to show that historic association is not a valid criterion for keeping harmful practices. Anti-pattern: retaining orthographic 'tradition' despite clear detriment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of word choice under per-word payment
rubrics_metrics.description: When paid by the word, prefer short (simple) words over long ones to maximize earnings for fixed writing labor/time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: a magazine contract paying 'seven cents a word' prompts Twain to argue he deliberately uses short words ('city' instead of 'metropolis', 'cop' instead of 'policeman') to increase words-per-page and thus pay. He computes word/letter counts to show how long words reduce his income. Practical guidance: choose shorter synonyms when compensated per word; calculate average word length to estimate value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecturing tactics to manage stage-fright and audience reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use preparation, staged support, and fallback materials to control stage-fright and shape audience response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the 'first appearance' account: place supportive friends in the audience instructed to react (pound clubs, deliver a laugh) to cue the crowd; tuck a manuscript under a flag as a safety; pace (walk) to steady nerves. These are tactical measures for a successful public performance and for overcoming initial fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid personal anecdotes with explicit morals in speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal, often comic or self-deprecating memories should be used as illustrative anecdotes that end with an explicit moral or lesson for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 'Morals and Memory' Twain strings together episodic memories (stealing/extracting a watermelon, fishing and finding a corpse, boots incident) and frames each as having a moral or lesson. Guidance: select memorable, concrete incidents that naturally yield a moral and that connect emotionally with listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical interpersonal advice for authors (retain counsel)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is service to an author to have a lawyer; authors should work through legal counsel in dealings with publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain remarks from the Authors' Club address that having a lawyer is protective and advises authors to use lawyers for publisher relations—even humorously noting he 'never made anything out of him.' This is pragmatic professional advice rather than stylistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical technique: flatter and thank key intermediaries (booksellers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing intermediaries (e.g., booksellers), use gratitude, concrete sales figures, and praise to strengthen relations and acknowledge their role in an author's livelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Booksellers address Twain gives detailed yearly sales statistics, praises the audience's role in selling older titles, and thanks them for their work. Guidance: employ specific numbers and sincere gratitude as rhetorical tools to cement partnerships and goodwill.
